{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"b07142f5c0733c4ca746bebab38c3e6517fab0cf829a77d7d175f20668f8f0c6","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:68","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sharing the road","heading":"C — Bicycles, pedestrians, trucks and no-zones, recreational vehicles and trailers, motorcycles and mopeds, moped law and registration, and littering (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Bicycles, pedestrians, trucks and no-zones, recreational vehicles and trailers, motorcycles and mopeds, moped law and registration, and littering (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: how North Carolina drivers share the road with bicyclists, pedestrians, large trucks, recreational vehicles, trailers, motorcycles and mopeds, the state's bicycle and moped equipment, age and registration rules, and the littering law.

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A01
North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists must obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A01
Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway, and traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A01
Bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane, choosing based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A01
Like drivers, bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road, stop for stop signs and red lights, and give hand signals. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A02
Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane; changing lanes is the safest way to pass. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A02
Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A02
Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A02
At night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least 300 feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least 200 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A02
Expect bicycles on every road except where they are expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook collisions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A02
Every bicycle rider and passenger under age 16 must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A02
A bicycle passenger under 40 pounds or under 40 inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A03
In cities about 2 of every 5 people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about 1 in 10 in rural areas. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A03
Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A03
On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see you. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A03
Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A03
A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn; check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A03
Truck brakes heat up on downhill runs, which means the truck needs more distance to stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A03
Wind currents from a large truck beside you can affect your steering, so give trucks plenty of room. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A03
Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A04
A tractor-trailer's no-zones reach up to 20 feet in front of the cab, along both sides especially beside the cab, and up to 200 feet behind. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A04
Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger; if you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A04
Recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F24 | anchor: A04
The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F25 | anchor: A04
Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F26 | anchor: A04
Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F27 | anchor: A04
Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F28 | anchor: A04
A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F29 | anchor: A04
Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least 2 feet to its left. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F30 | anchor: A04
Leave enough room when passing any cyclist so your vehicle's windstream cannot make the rider lose control. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F31 | anchor: A04
Motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially when turning left. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F32 | anchor: A05
About two-thirds of North Carolina motorcycle crashes involve a car, and in most of them the car driver is at fault, often saying the motorcycle went unseen. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F33 | anchor: A05
Moped riders and all passengers must wear a helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 218 with the retention strap fastened. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F34 | anchor: A05
Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F35 | anchor: A05
Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water on the pavement can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F36 | anchor: A05
Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads because two wheels are easily destabilized. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F37 | anchor: A05
Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F38 | anchor: A05
North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than 50 cubic centimeters and no external shifting device. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F39 | anchor: A05
A moped's top speed may not exceed 30 mph, and mopeds built to go faster are illegal to use in North Carolina. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F40 | anchor: A05
To operate a moped on a public road you must be at least 16 and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card, and impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec16-F41 | anchor: A06
Moped riders should keep right in the lane, never share a lane with another vehicle, and never squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic at an intersection. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec16-F42 | anchor: A06
Moped riders should wear light or bright clothing and use electric turn signals if fitted, or hand signals otherwise. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec16-F43 | anchor: A06
Since July 2015, every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec16-F44 | anchor: A06
Moped registration costs $29.50 a year, and a few counties add a transit tax. [A06]
Why it matters: dynamic fact; fees can change.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec16-F45 | anchor: A06
A moped owner without the manufacturer's certificate of origin can use form MVR-58, an affidavit of facts, as proof of ownership. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec16-F46 | anchor: A07
Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec16-F47 | anchor: A07
A first littering conviction carries a fine of $250 to $1,000, and a repeat offense within 3 years carries $500 to $2,000. [A07]
Why it matters: dynamic fact; fine amounts are set by law and can change.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0097]

Misconceptions: bicyclists are not required to stay on the shoulder and may use the full lane; pedestrians walk facing traffic while bicyclists ride with it; a high truck cab does not mean the trucker can see you; a motorcycle does not have to share its lane when you pass; a moped built to exceed the legal top speed is not legal just because it is sold; the driver, not only the passenger who threw it, answers for litter from the vehicle.
Mnemonics: bikes ride with traffic, walkers face traffic; no mirror, no driver, no-zone; full lane for a motorcycle, keep a gap when passing a moped; moped means small motor, low top speed, licensed rider.
Glossary: no-zone means a large blind area around a truck where a car disappears from the trucker's view; bicycle restraining seat means the special seat a small bicycle passenger must ride in; jackknife means a trailer swinging sideways against the towing vehicle; moped means a small-motor two- or three-wheeler with a limited top speed; certificate of origin means the manufacturer's document used as proof of moped ownership at registration.
Dynamic facts: moped registration fees, county transit taxes and littering fines can change and are flagged as dynamic.
